1331.title: Sita calls the fire as witness
1331.hook: after the war Sita answers Rama, then calls Agni as her witness; why Hindus still make vows before the fire
1331.carry: the fire is the witness of truth
1331.howItsDone: Sita's ordeal by fire, the agni pariksha, is retold, staged and debated across Hindu traditions; and at Hindu weddings couples still circle the sacred fire, making their vows with Agni as witness.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sita kept her dharma even as a captive in the ashoka grove: a blade of grass between her and Ravana, and a no to Hanuman's offer of a ride home.
screen: `SITA KEPT HER DHARMA, EVEN CAPTIVE.`

segments.voice: The war is over. Ravana is dead. Sita is brought out in front of the whole army, and the reunion the story has been moving toward doesn't come. In Valmiki's sixth book, Rama speaks to her coldly, in public. He says, in paraphrase, that he fought to clear his name and his family's, and that she may go wherever she likes. It's a hard scene to read. Today isn't about defending it or explaining it away. It's about the woman who has to answer it, and what she says.
screen: `THE WAR IS OVER.` → `NO REUNION, A COLD SPEECH.` → `WHAT SITA SAYS BACK.`

segments.voice: Sita doesn't stay silent. She wipes her tears and speaks, and Valmiki gives her a full answer. In paraphrase: why do you speak to me like this, the way a common man speaks to a common woman? What was in my power, my heart, was always yours. What was not in my power, my body seized by force, was not my doing. If you meant to give me up, why didn't you say so when Hanuman came? I would have ended my life then, and spared you a war. Then she asks Lakshmana to build a fire. She faces the flames and calls on Agni, the god of fire, in paraphrase: as my heart has never strayed from Rama, may Agni, the witness of the world, protect me. And she steps in. Agni rises carrying her, gives her back, and declares her faultless. Here's the teaching inside the scene. Agni is the fire of every Vedic offering, and in the epics he is the witness: earlier in this same story, Rama and Sugriva seal their friendship by walking around a fire. That's why, at a Hindu wedding, the couple circles the sacred fire and make their vows before it; families call it agni sakshi, the fire as witness. Sita didn't ask the army to vouch for her. She called the witness her whole tradition trusts. The tradition still wrestles with this scene: many read the fire as her victory, and Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas tells it so the real Sita was never in Lanka at all.
screen: `SHE WIPES HER TEARS AND SPEAKS` · `MY HEART WAS ALWAYS YOURS` · `AGNI, WITNESS OF THE WORLD` · `WHY WEDDINGS CIRCLE THE FIRE`

segments.voice: Many Hindu homes light a small lamp, a diya, when they pray. Light one, or a candle, somewhere safe, or just picture a flame. Let it be your witness for a few breaths, and say one true thing before it, silently: something that's yours, that you'd stand behind in front of anyone. If you pray, offer it to God, as Sita offered her truth to Agni. And if a weight ever feels like more than you can carry, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.

1332.title: Draupadi's secret was no charm
1332.hook: Krishna's wife asks Draupadi for a love charm, and Draupadi answers with the householder's real work
1332.howItsDone: Hindus meet Draupadi in retellings of the Mahabharata, in storytelling and theater, and in some regions as a goddess with her own temples and festivals; her conversation with Satyabhama is read in many ways, from a model of devotion to a portrait of a capable queen.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fire is the witness of truth kept her dharma even as a captive answered Rama in front of the army, then asked for a fire. Now the other epic.
screen: `THE FIRE IS THE WITNESS OF TRUTH KEPT HER DHARMA EVEN AS A CAPTIVE.`

segments.voice: The question is a little rude, and the guest asks it anyway. The Pandavas are living in the forest, and Krishna comes to visit with his wife Satyabhama. While the men talk, the two women sit together. Satyabhama leans in. Your husbands are heroes, she says, in paraphrase, and they never cross you. How do you do it? Is it a vow? A mantra? Some herb, some charm? Tell me, so Krishna will be like that with me. Draupadi could laugh, or be offended. Instead she gives a long answer, with no magic in it at all. Today: Draupadi, at home.
screen: `A GUEST IN THE FOREST.` → `WHAT'S YOUR SECRET CHARM?` → `AN ANSWER WITH NO MAGIC IN IT.`

segments.voice: Draupadi starts by refusing the premise. Charms and potions, she says in the epic's Forest Book, are a road to ruin. A husband who learns his wife is working spells on him grows afraid of her, the way a person fears a snake in the house. Then she tells Satyabhama what she actually does, and it reads like a day's work. She sets her pride aside. She rises before the household and sleeps after it. She sees that guests are fed and the servants looked after. Then a line some readers stop on: back at Indraprastha, the brothers left the household's income and spending to her. She alone kept track of it. The woman remembered from the dice hall was also the one who knew where the kingdom's money went. Here's the teaching. Hinduism names four stages of life: student, householder, forest-dweller, renunciant. The householder, the grihastha, isn't the lesser one. The law book of Manu says that as every creature lives by the air, the other stages live by the householder: the house feeds the student, the guest, the wandering monk. So the work Draupadi lists isn't beneath dharma. It is dharma, done daily. Readers still argue over the speech. Some hear devotion, some a capable queen, some are uneasy with an ideal built around serving. And she says it all in exile, with no palace left, from memory, without complaint.
screen: `CHARMS ARE A ROAD TO RUIN` · `A DAY'S WORK, NOT A SPELL` · `SHE KEPT THE KINGDOM'S ACCOUNTS` · `GRIHASTHA: THE HOUSEHOLDER'S DHARMA`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ordinary day in your home, or a home you grew up in, and ask who kept it running: the food, the bills, the guests, the small repairs. Hindus call that work grihastha dharma, the householder's path. Let one person come to mind, maybe you, and let each breath out thank them silently for it. If you pray, you can name them before God.
Draupadi. Asked for a charm, she described the householder's work, down to a kingdom's accounts. Today's word.
screen: `DRAUPADI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the householder's work is dharma. Draupadi's secret was never a charm. Until tomorrow.

1333.title: Krishna eats the last leaf
1333.hook: the pot is empty, a famously angry sage is coming, and Krishna arrives asking for food; why Hindus offer food to God first
1333.carry: a leaf offered with love is enough for God
1333.howItsDone: Hindus hear the story of Durvasa's visit in retellings of the Mahabharata and in devotional storytelling; and in many homes a little food is offered to God before the meal, then shared as prasad.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the householder's work is dharma at home: asked for a charm, she gave a list of chores and remembered keeping the accounts at Indraprastha.
screen: `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S WORK IS DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Dinner is over. The plates are washed. The cook has finally sat down and eaten her own meal. Then there's a knock. A great sage is at the door, with a crowd of disciples behind him, and they would like to be fed. They're going down to the river to bathe first. They'll be back soon. Hungry. In the forest years of the Mahabharata, this is Draupadi's evening, and the sage is Durvasa, remembered for his temper and his curses. Today: an empty pot, and the guest who scraped it.
screen: `THE MEAL IS OVER.` → `A SAGE AT THE DOOR, WITH DISCIPLES.` → `AN EMPTY POT.`

segments.voice: First, the pot. Early in the exile, the sun gives Yudhishthira a vessel that will feed the household and its guests every day, until Draupadi has eaten. So Draupadi serves everyone first and eats last. Some tellings carry the next part. Duryodhana, hoping to trap his cousins, sends Durvasa at exactly the wrong hour, after Draupadi has eaten. The sage and his disciples go off to bathe. Draupadi has nothing to give them, and a sage refused hospitality might curse the house. So she turns to Krishna in her mind, and Krishna arrives. His first words, in paraphrase: I'm hungry. Give me something to eat. The pot is empty, she tells him; that's why I called you. He asks to see it anyway. Stuck to the rim is one small scrap of cooked greens, a bit of leaf. Krishna eats it, and says, may this satisfy the one who is the soul of the world. Down at the river, the sages suddenly feel full, as if they'd eaten a feast, and slip away. Here's the teaching. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says it plainly, in paraphrase: whoever offers me a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with love, I accept it. In this story he shows it: one leaf, from a woman with nothing left, and the soul of the world is satisfied. That's why, in many Hindu homes, a little of the meal is set before God first, naivedya, and then shared as prasad, blessed food. The size of the offering was never the point.
screen: `A VESSEL THAT FEEDS UNTIL SHE EATS` · `KRISHNA COMES ASKING FOR FOOD` · `ONE LEAF ON THE RIM` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER`

segments.voice: At your next meal, before the first bite, set aside a small portion, a spoonful, a piece of fruit, and offer it silently, the way many Hindu families do; then eat it or share it as prasad. Some families say a short verse from the Gita before eating, brahmarpanam, offering the meal back to God; others simply say Krishna's name. If you don't pray, just pause and thank everyone whose work is on the plate.
Draupadi. When the pot was empty and guests were coming, Krishna made a meal of the one leaf on its rim. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: a leaf offered with love is enough for God. Krishna ate the last one. I'll be here tomorrow.

1334.title: Draupadi spares her sons' killer
1334.hook: her sons' killer is dragged before her in ropes, and in the Bhagavata she asks for his life: kshama, mercy that doesn't erase the harm
1334.carry: kshama, forbearance, is a mark of dharma
1334.howItsDone: Hindus who read or hear the Bhagavata Purana meet this scene early in its first book, sometimes in long public recitations, and storytellers set it beside the Mahabharata's own telling.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a leaf offered with love is enough for God: the pot was empty, and Krishna arrived hungry and made a meal of the one leaf on the rim.
screen: `A LEAF OFFERED WITH LOVE IS ENOUGH FOR GOD.`

segments.voice: Ropes around his arms, Ashvatthama is pushed forward and made to stand in front of her. He is the son of Drona, the Pandavas' own teacher. On the last night of the war he crept into their sleeping camp and killed Draupadi's sons. Arjuna has caught him and tied him up like an animal. Krishna has told Arjuna he may kill him. Instead, Arjuna brings him to the mother of the dead. Last year on this path, the Mahabharata's telling of this moment ended with a jewel. Today the Bhagavata Purana tells it, and she says something else.
screen: `THE KILLER, IN ROPES.` → `BROUGHT TO THE MOTHER.` → `THE BHAGAVATA TELLS IT.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana's first book, Draupadi sees the son of her husbands' teacher bound and ashamed, and she bows to him. Then she speaks, in paraphrase. Let him go. He is the son of the teacher from whom you learned your bows and weapons; in him, the teacher is still here. Then the line the scene turns on: his mother, Kripi, is still alive. Don't let her weep the way I am weeping now. The text calls her words fair, kind and full of dharma. Bhima does not agree: this man killed sleeping children, he says, and deserves to die. Krishna finds a way through. Arjuna cuts the jewel from Ashvatthama's head and shaves his hair, a punishment the text treats as a kind of death for one like him, and sends him out alive. In the Mahabharata's own telling, Draupadi asks for the jewel; in the Bhagavata, she asks for his life. Readers have held both. Here's the teaching. Hinduism has a word for what she does: kshama, forbearance, the strength not to strike back when you could. The law book of Manu lists it among the ten marks of dharma, beside truth and freedom from anger. And notice what kshama isn't. Her grief doesn't vanish; she names it. The punishment still falls. She doesn't ask what he deserves. She asks who else will be sitting where she is sitting tonight.
screen: `SHE BOWS TO THE BOUND MAN` · `LET HIS MOTHER NOT WEEP AS I DO` · `KSHAMA: A MARK OF DHARMA` · `MERCY, AND THE PUNISHMENT STILL FALLS`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who hurt you, small or large; you don't have to forgive them in this sit, and kshama never means the harm didn't happen. Just look past the person, once, to someone who loves them, a mother, a child, a friend, and let that person be there for a few breaths. If you pray, you can hold that other person in prayer. If the hurt is still happening, or grief is too much, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.
Draupadi. In the Bhagavata, with her sons' killer in ropes before her, she asks for his life so that his mother won't weep as she does. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: kshama, forbearance, is a mark of dharma. Draupadi saw another mother. See you tomorrow.

segments.voice: Call when you get there. Come back soon. Those are goodbye requests. The war is over, the Pandavas are on the throne, and Krishna's chariot is ready to take him home to Dvaraka. His aunt Kunti, the mother of the Pandavas, comes out to see him off. She has lost a husband, hidden in forests, seen her sons gambled into exile and then sent to war. She has finally reached a quiet season. And at the chariot she asks him for something hard to imagine wanting. Today: Kunti, and the gift she wanted.
screen: `A GOODBYE AT THE CHARIOT.` → `A HARD LIFE, A QUIET SEASON.` → `A STRANGE REQUEST.`

segments.voice: The scene sits in the first book of the Bhagavata Purana, and devotees know it as Kunti's prayer. She begins by remembering. You saved us, she tells Krishna, in paraphrase: from poison, from the house of lac, from the forest, from the dice hall, from the weapons of great warriors. Then the request. In Sanskrit it begins vipadah santu tah shashvat: let those troubles come again and again. Why? Because in trouble we saw you, and seeing you is the end of the round of births. She goes further. Wealth, birth, learning and beauty, she says, can make a person too proud to call on God. Those who have nothing are the ones who turn to him. Here's the teaching. This is bhakti, loving devotion, at its most daring. Most prayers ask God for something. Kunti asks for God himself, and for whatever keeps her looking at him, even over comfort. And she isn't romanticizing pain; she lists exactly what the hard years cost. She's saying what she found inside them. It's a reading, not a rule. Some devotional teachers call this prayer the heart of surrender. Other readers are wary of wishing hardship on anyone, and say Kunti speaks for herself, not for every sufferer. And she ends gently, asking Krishna to cut the ties of affection that bind her, so her mind can flow toward him like a river to the sea.
screen: `SHE REMEMBERS EVERY DANGER` · `LET THOSE TROUBLES COME AGAIN` · `IN TROUBLE, WE SAW YOU` · `BHAKTI: GOD OVER COMFORT`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one difficult stretch of your life that's over now, and without reliving the worst of it, ask gently where you turned then, and what you saw: a friend who showed up, a strength, a clarity. You don't have to wish it back, as Kunti did; just let what you found sit with you for a few breaths. If you pray, do what Kunti did: name God in that memory, and give thanks for what you were shown.

segments.voice: Through a thin wall, in a borrowed room, a mother hears another family crying. Years before the war, after the house of lac burned, Kunti and her sons are hiding in a town called Ekachakra, dressed as poor brahmins, living with a brahmin family who took them in. One evening the house fills with weeping. Kunti goes to find out why. Tomorrow, the family tells her, it's their turn. A demon named Baka lives near the town, and each household in turn must send him a cart of food and a person to be eaten with it. Now they're arguing over who should go. Today: what Kunti says next.
screen: `A BORROWED ROOM IN EKACHAKRA.` → `THE HOST FAMILY WEEPS.` → `IT'S THEIR TURN TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: The scene is in the Mahabharata's first book, and it starts with the family. The father says he will go. The mother says no, she will; the children need their father more. The daughter says send me. And the small son picks up a blade of grass, waves it, and says he'll kill the demon with that. Then Kunti speaks, in paraphrase. You have sheltered us; let me repay you. I have five sons, and one of them will take the food to Baka. The brahmin refuses. He can't let a guest die for him. Kunti insists: the son she has in mind is strong. When the brothers come home, Yudhishthira is upset: you're risking our brother on a stranger's trouble? Kunti is calm. She has seen Bhima's strength since he was a baby. And repaying the people who sheltered them, she says, is dharma. So Bhima goes, eats the demon's food in front of him to make him angry, and kills him. Here's the teaching. Hinduism has a word for what Kunti is weighing: rina, debt. The Vedic texts say a person is born owing debts, to the gods, to the sages, to the ancestors; and the householder's daily duties include caring for people, the guest above all. Kunti is the guest here, and she owes. To her, paying it back isn't generosity she can skip. It's dharma. Her eldest questions her. The decision is hers.
screen: `EACH ONE OFFERS TO GO` · `LET ME REPAY YOU` · `RINA: THE DEBTS WE'RE BORN WITH` · `REPAYING THE HOUSE IS DHARMA`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a time someone took you in, a room, a meal, a ride, a hand when you needed it, and let their face come clearly. Hold them with each breath. Then let one small way to repay that kindness come to mind, a call, a meal, an hour of help, the way Hindu families have long answered kindness with food and time. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name.

segments.voice: Krishna's peace mission has failed. Before he leaves Hastinapura, he goes to see his aunt, who has stayed behind in the city while her sons waited out their exile. He asks if she has a message for them. She does, but she doesn't start with advice. She starts with a story, an old one, she says, about a woman named Vidula and her son. Kunti wants her sons to hear it before the war. Today, at the end of a week of the epics' women, Kunti speaks through someone else's voice.
screen: `THE PEACE MISSION HAS FAILED.` → `A MESSAGE FOR HER SONS.` → `SHE TELLS THEM A STORY.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Mahabharata's Book of Effort, here in paraphrase. Vidula is a proud woman of a warrior family. Her son Sanjaya has been beaten by a rival king, and now he lies at home, low and listless. Vidula goes to him, and she is not gentle. Get up, she tells him. You were not born to lie here. Then this line, which in Sanskrit runs muhurtam jvalitam shreyo, na tu dhumayitam ciram: better to blaze up for a moment than to smolder for a long time. Her son argues back: what good is a kingdom to you if I'm dead? She answers him again and again until he rises. Then Kunti adds her own words for Arjuna and Bhima: the time has come for which a mother of warriors bears sons. Here's the teaching. Hindus call it svadharma, your own duty, the one that's yours by your stage of life and where you stand. Soon after, on the battlefield, Krishna tells Arjuna nearly the same thing in the Bhagavad Gita: don't give in to weakness; stand up. And: better your own dharma, done imperfectly, than another's done well. Some readers hear courage; others hear the cost of a war a mother has just urged. The epic keeps both. And it closes a week of women: Sita, Draupadi, and Kunti, who sends a story ahead of her sons.
screen: `VIDULA AND HER BEATEN SON` · `BLAZE A MOMENT, DON'T SMOLDER` · `SVADHARMA: YOUR OWN DUTY` · `THE GITA: STAND UP`

segments.voice: Ask gently what is yours to do right now, as a student, a parent, a friend, a worker, and whether one part of it has been smoldering a long time. Don't scold yourself: Vidula's words were for a warrior, and yours can be kinder. Let it come into view, warmth gathering around it like an ember on each breath in, one first step appearing on each breath out. If you pray, you can ask for courage. And if low days ever start to feel like there's no point, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.
